sense: money set aside for a purpose

evidence: Liv. 1.53.3: captīvam pecūniam in aedificātiōnem ejus templī sēposuit
Cic. Att. 15.15.3: id ego ad illud fānum sēpositum putābam
Levi–Bini p. 28: pecūnia for fondo, money meant for a purpose
terms.comment: Latin names the money and what it is put aside for: pecūniam in rem sēpōnere.

terms.gloss: a treasury; a fund held in common
evidence: Nep. Arist. 3.1: id enim commūne aerārium esse voluērunt
Liv. 27.10.11: in sānctiōre aerāriō, the reserve kept for the worst emergencies
terms.comment: Classically the state treasury in the temple of Saturn, and so any fund held in common: the Delian League’s, or the fund Augustus set up to pay soldiers on their discharge (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: captīvam pecūniam in aedificātiōnem ejus templī sēposuit
phrases.english: he set the captured money aside for building the temple

phrases.latin: Id enim commūne aerārium esse voluērunt.
phrases.english: For they wanted this to be their common fund.

phrases.latin: aerārium mīlitāre cum vectīgālibus novīs cōnstituit
phrases.english: he set up a fund for the soldiers, with new taxes to keep it filled

sources: Lewis & Short: pecunia · Lewis & Short: sepono · Lewis & Short: aerarium
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 28 (fondo).
